t: Introduction: topic and aim of the session
n: In this session we will examine the liability of the doctor. In his work, the doctor is answerable in three areas: labour, that is, disciplinary; administrative; and civil-law. The plan is as follows: the employment contract, working time, occupational safety, termination of the contract and disciplinary penalty. Then administrative offences, and then the question of compensation for harm. Attention: being held to disciplinary, administrative or criminal liability does not release the doctor from compensating for harm. Civil liability is preserved separately.

t: Foundations of labour legislation and the prohibition of forced labour
n: According to Article 37 of the Constitution, a citizen has the right to work, to freely choose a job, to work under fair conditions and to protection against unemployment. The Labour Code is the main source of labour law and regulates labour relations in accordance with the principles of a market economy. Labour law governs the establishment, change and termination of relations on the basis of a contract, as well as pay, discipline, occupational safety and labour disputes. Compelling a person to work under threat of punishment is prohibited. Military or alternative service, work in a state of emergency and work under a court sentence are not forced labour.

t: Specific features of labour relations
n: Labour relations differ from the subject matter of branches such as civil law by their specific features. The table gives four features. The first: labour creates value in production. The second: the employee is a member of a collective and has definite rights and duties. The third: labour is paid activity that satisfies a need. Payment distinguishes labour from activities performed on a public basis. The fourth: the citizen takes part in the work personally and performs work in a defined profession or post.

t: Rights of the employee and the employer
n: The employee also has the right to rest, vocational training and professional development; this is stated in Article 16 of the Labour Code. The employee may be a member of a trade union and, in cases provided by law, receive social security. The employee's rights include pay not lower than the minimum wage, safe and hygienic conditions, judicial protection and legal aid. The employer, for its part, has the right to conclude and terminate contracts and to demand full performance of the work. Attention: Article 16 gives the rights of the employee, and Article 17 the rights of the employer. Do not confuse the articles.

t: Duties of the employee and the employer
n: Duties of the employee: to work honestly and conscientiously, to observe labour discipline, to carry out a lawful order on time, and to protect the employer's property. The employee must also observe the requirements of safety engineering and occupational safety, which is in Article 176. The employer organises the work, creates the conditions stipulated in the contract, observes the rules of discipline and protection, and concludes collective agreements. The employer has no right to demand from the employee work that is not part of his job duties. Nor can the employer demand actions that are unlawful, dangerous to life and health, or degrading to honour.

t: Employment contract: content and terms
n: The employment contract specifies the place of work, the job function, the post, the start time of work and the amount of pay. A fixed-term contract also states the period of its validity. The level of labour rights and guarantees established by law cannot be lowered by the contract. On terms: if no term is stated, the contract is considered concluded for an indefinite period. A definite term must not exceed five years. A contract for a specific piece of work is designed for the time needed to perform the work. When a contract is renewed, it cannot be changed without the employee's consent.

t: Hiring: documents and probation
n: On hiring, the passport, work record book, military registration document, and diploma or document of special training are presented. A work record book is not required of those taking up work for the first time; part-time workers provide a certificate. Probation is established to test the employee's fitness for the work and to determine whether continuing the work is appropriate. The probation period is up to 3 months, according to Article 85. Cancelling probation requires 3 days' notice. Probation is not set for a pregnant woman, nor for a woman with a child under 3 years of age.

t: Quick questions: contract and hiring
n: Now for quick questions. What is the maximum length of probation? It is set for a period not exceeding three months. What if the period of validity is not stated in the contract? It is considered concluded for an indefinite period. Is probation set for a pregnant woman? No, it is not set for pregnant women or for women with children under three years of age. Attention, there is a risk of error: a fixed-term contract does not exceed 5 years. The probation period is 3 months, while the notice of cancelling probation is 3 days; do not confuse these two figures.

t: Collective agreement
n: A collective agreement regulates the relations of the employer and the employees; its parties are the trade union and the employer. Terms more favourable than those in the law are possible: additional leave, a pension supplement, compensation payments. The draft is discussed at a general meeting. When its term expires, it remains in force until a new one is concluded. The principles of Article 30 of the Labour Code fall into three groups: legality, that is, compliance with legal norms and competence; freedom, that is, choice of the question and voluntary obligation; and control, that is, performance, supervision and liability.

t: Part-time work, several professions and substitution
n: Part-time work is paid work performed under a contract in time free from the main job. Internal part-time work is performed in one's own institution, external part-time work in another institution. Working in several professions means working in another post alongside the main one; this is possible only when the volume of the main job is fully performed within the main working time. In substitution, the work of an absent employee is performed while his post is retained. The head of a health care institution is permitted to work as a doctor, and a doctor as a mid-level medical worker.

t: Working time and the shortened time of medical workers
n: Working time is the time during which the employee must perform the job function according to the schedule or contract. Normal working time is 40 hours per week; 8 hours a day in a five-day week and 7 hours a day in a six-day week. For some categories it is shortened without reducing pay: persons under 18, disabled persons of groups I-II, those working in unfavourable conditions, and others. For work involving high emotional and nervous strain, up to 36 hours per week is set; medical workers belong to this category.

t: Occupational safety and medical examinations
n: The employer creates conditions meeting safety and hygiene requirements and is responsible for this. On hiring, he informs the employee of the hazards and means of protection. The employee observes the requirements of occupational safety, uses protective equipment, and reports a dangerous situation or an accident without delay. Particular categories, that is, persons under 18, disabled persons, those on night work and those serving the public, undergo preliminary and periodic examination. Refusal becomes a ground for suspension from work. If the employee considers that deterioration of his health is related to working conditions, he demands an extraordinary examination. The employee does not pay the cost of the examination.

t: Termination of the contract on the employee's initiative
n: The employee is entitled to terminate a fixed-term or open-ended contract by warning the employer in writing two weeks in advance. The stages: first, a written warning to the employer 2 weeks in advance. Second, until the notice period ends, the employee may withdraw his application. Third, if the contract is not terminated after the period has passed, the application loses force. Fourth, on departure the record book is issued and final settlement is made. Exception: for reasons such as admission to study, retirement or elections, the employer terminates the contract within the period the employee requests.

t: Grounds for termination on the employer's initiative
n: The employer terminates the contract only for the reasons in the Labour Code and in strict compliance with all formal requirements. Organisational grounds: staff reduction or liquidation of the enterprise. Grounds relating to the employee: insufficient qualification or unfitness because of health. Other grounds: part-time workers, and the manager on a change of owner. Systematic violation: repeated misconduct within 1 year after a penalty. A single gross violation is assessed according to its consequences. Attention: the contract cannot be terminated during temporary incapacity for work or leave; this is possible only if the enterprise is liquidated entirely.

t: Notice periods for termination
n: The employer warns the employee of the intention to terminate in writing, against signature; the period differs depending on the ground. For staff reduction or liquidation, at least 2 months in advance. For unfitness because of qualification or health, at least 2 weeks in advance. For systematic violation, 3 days in advance. For a single gross violation, also 3 days in advance. In reduction and unfitness, by agreement, the warning is replaced by monetary compensation. Attention: on the employee's initiative the period is two weeks; on the employer's initiative it depends on the ground.

t: Disciplinary penalties and the procedure for applying them
n: Types of disciplinary penalty: reprimand, a fine of up to 30% of the average monthly wage, and termination of the employment contract. Under the internal regulations, for some offences the fine may be set at up to 50% of the monthly wage. Before the penalty, a written explanation is requested. One penalty is imposed for one violation, and it is announced by order. Time limits: the penalty is applied within 1 month, no later than 6 months without an audit, and no later than 2 years with an audit. The penalty remains in effect for 1 year.

t: Case analysis: labour legislation
n: Case analysis. Situation: a polyclinic doctor refused to undergo a periodic medical examination and did not follow the doctors' recommendations. Analysis: refusing the examination or not following the recommendations is a ground for suspending the employee from work. The employee does not pay the cost of the examination. Attention: in staff reduction the employer warns in writing at least 2 months in advance, and in unfitness at least 2 weeks in advance. During illness and leave the contract cannot be terminated. Think about it: what decision will the employer take in the first case? In the second case, if the employee falls ill, can the contract be terminated?

t: Administrative legislation and administrative offence
n: Administrative legislation regulates public relations in state administration and other fields. It also includes sanitary rules and licensing rules. An administrative offence is a culpable action or omission that infringes the rights of citizens, property, public order or the natural environment; fault takes the form of intent or negligence. Attention: an administrative offence is not a crime. It does not carry signs of danger to society, and therefore criminal liability does not arise. However, if the consequence of violating sanitary and anti-epidemic rules is grave or social danger arises, it may be assessed as a crime.

t: Administrative legislation: right and duty
n: Administrative legislation is an independent branch: a body of documents regulating public relations in state administration and other fields. It sets the rules of conduct for institutions, officials and citizens: sanitary rules, licensing rules and others. The Constitution establishes, together with the rights and freedoms of citizens, the equality of their duties as well. The logic is this: a lawful action is the exercise of a right. Failure to perform a duty, however, becomes grounds for measures provided by law. An unlawful action, that is, a violation of a norm of administrative law, brings administrative coercion.

t: Intent, negligence, extreme necessity and age
n: In committing an act intentionally, the person knows his action is unlawful and desires the harmful consequence or consciously allows it. In negligence, the person frivolously thinks the consequence can be avoided, or fails to foresee it. Extreme necessity is not an offence: if the harm caused is less, it is not considered an offence. Persons under 16 are not held to administrative liability. In a minor case, a warning is possible.

t: Types of administrative penalty and amounts of fines
n: Types of administrative penalty: fine, compensated seizure of an item, confiscation, deprivation of a special right, and administrative detention. For professional offences of medical workers a fine is mainly imposed. The limit of the fine is set relative to the minimum monthly wage. For a citizen, from one fiftieth to five times the minimum; for an official, from one tenth to ten times. In exceptional cases, up to one hundred times for a citizen and up to one hundred and fifty times for an official. Under a decision of a local authority, the fine does not exceed three times for a citizen and five times for an official.

t: Time limits for imposing a penalty and the bodies that consider cases
n: The penalty is imposed no later than two months from the day the offence was committed or, if it is continuing, from the day it was discovered. If a criminal case is refused or terminated, the penalty is imposed within one month from the decision. In confiscation by a customs body, these time limits do not apply. The case is considered by a judge, a commercial court, administrative commissions, internal affairs bodies and state inspectorates. Among them are also inspectors of State Sanitary Supervision and of state supervision of labour.

t: Quick questions: administrative liability
n: More quick questions. From what age does administrative liability begin? Persons who had not reached sixteen years at the time of the offence are not held liable. What are the types of administrative penalty? A fine, compensated seizure of an item, confiscation, deprivation of a special right, detention; a medical worker most often receives a fine. Attention: a fine is imposed on a citizen at from 1/50 to 5 times the minimum monthly wage, and on an official at from 1/10 to 10 times. The difference between intent and negligence: in intent, the person knows it is unlawful and desires the consequence or allows it; in negligence, he does not foresee it or hopes to prevent it.

t: Record of offence and the rights of the person being held liable
n: The record states the date, place, the essence of the offence, the regulatory document and the written explanation. The stages: a record is drawn up on the results of the inquiry; if signing is refused, a note of this is made; the case is considered with the person's participation, and an expert examination is ordered if necessary. According to Article 294 of the Code of Administrative Liability, the person being held liable has the right to see the case file, to a lawyer, to an interpreter, and to appeal. The victim also has rights.

t: Administrative offences in the work of medical workers
n: Offences such as slander and insult relate more to the work of heads of institutions. Under Articles 52-59, the subject of the offence may be a medical worker as well as other citizens. The groups: infringement of citizens' rights, Articles 40-43, 49, 51, slander, insult, the state language. Public health, Articles 52-59: sanitary, epidemic, radiation. Trade and entrepreneurship, Articles 164, 176 and others: paid services, contractual discipline. The order of administration, Articles 199, 215. Example: knowingly making a false call to the ambulance service relates to a citizen, while violating statistical reporting relates to an official.

t: Case analysis: administrative liability
n: Case analysis. Situation: an official of a district hospital did not submit the state statistical report in the established manner. This act is a ground for administrative liability. The subject of the offence is an official of the health care institution. The fine for an official must be not less than one tenth and not more than ten times the minimum monthly wage. Think about it: which type of penalty is applied in this case, and within how many months after the offence was committed may the penalty be imposed?

t: Civil law: concept, subjects and objects
n: Civil law is a system of norms regulating the property and related non-property relations of citizens and organisations. Subjects: natural persons, that is, citizens, foreigners, stateless persons, legal entities, and also the state and territorial formations. Legal capacity is the ability to have rights and duties. Capacity to act is the ability, by one's own actions, to acquire rights and to answer for them. Objects: things, money, work and services, results of intellectual activity. Honour, dignity and business reputation are non-property rights protected through the courts.

t: Tort and contractual liability
n: A tort is where the very fact of causing harm gives rise to the obligation to compensate it. A contract between the patient and the institution is rarely concluded, so in medicine tort is more common. An "iatrogenic tort" is an offence involving compensation for harm caused by the doctor to the patient; this was proposed by A. V. Tikhomirov. The differences: in tort, unlawfulness is determined by general objective criteria, while in contractual liability only by breach of a contract term. The amount of harm in tort is determined by general rules; in contractual liability it is not less than in tort and may be increased.

t: Conditions of liability for harm and the presumption of fault
n: The fault of a medical worker takes two forms: intent or negligence, that is, carelessness or overconfidence. Civil law provides for a presumption of fault: the victim does not have to prove the fault of the person who caused the harm. If medical care was of poor quality, the burden of proving the absence of fault falls on the person who allowed the defect. The chain of liability: the fact that harm was caused, an unlawful action, a causal link, the fault of the person who caused the harm, and as a result the obligation to compensate the harm.

t: Harm from defects in goods, work and services (Civil Code 1017-1020)
n: If a design, formulation or other defect, or incorrect or insufficient information, causes harm to life, health or property, this harm is compensated, Civil Code 1017. The harm is compensated by the seller or manufacturer, that is, the performer, regardless of whether there was a contract. Harm from a defect in a product is compensated, at the victim's choice, by the seller or manufacturer, and harm from a defect in a service by the performer, Civil Code 1018. If force majeure or violation of the rules by the consumer is proved, the responsible person is released, Civil Code 1020.

t: Cases of finding no guilt, recourse and insurance
n: A medical worker is found not guilty if force majeure is proved; if the harm was caused at the patient's request or with his consent; or if the patient showed gross negligence. In such a dispute, medical records are decisive: the original, the completeness of the data in the daily notes, the absence of corrections. Civil Code 989: harm caused by an employee in performing his duties is compensated by the legal entity or citizen. Civil Code 992: if the insurance sum is insufficient, the difference is paid by the person responsible. Civil Code 1001, recourse: the institution that paid the compensation may demand the sum paid from the employee, but in practice such claims are very rare.

t: Quick questions: civil-law liability
n: Quick questions. First: must the patient prove the doctor's fault? No, the presumption of fault applies, and the doctor himself proves his lack of fault. Second: if extreme necessity releases from criminal liability, is the harm compensated? Yes, the harm must be paid; the court may place the obligation on another person. Third: if the institution has paid for harm caused by an employee, can it demand the money from the employee? Yes, there is a right of recourse, but in practice it is rarely used. Fourth: if the harm was caused with the patient's consent, why may the doctor be found not guilty? This shows how important it is to obtain informed consent.

t: Types of harm and the limitation period
n: Let us turn to the types of harm. Actual damage is the expenses incurred for treatment, medicines, sanatorium care and additional nutrition. Lost profit is wages and income. In compensating harm, the court relies on the conclusion of a medical-labour examination and, in a disputed case, a forensic medical examination. The general limitation period is three years, Civil Code 150; it runs from the day the person learned of the violation of the right.

t: Provision of medical care under a contract
n: A contract is an agreement of two or more persons to establish civil rights and duties. In a paid service, the performer provides the service and the customer pays for it, Article 703 of the Civil Code. If the performer does not perform the service, he pays for the harm, but not more than twice the price of the service, Civil Code 706. The conditions for terminating the contract are in Civil Code 707: the customer pays the full price of the service, and the performer fully compensates the customer's losses. The condition of paying the price where the performer is at fault, and of paying losses where the customer is at fault, does not apply.

t: Contract: freedom and paid services (Civil Code 353-355)
n: A contract is an agreement of two or more persons to establish, change or terminate civil rights and duties, Civil Code 353. There is freedom in concluding a contract; compelling a person to conclude one is not permitted, except in cases provided by law, Civil Code 354. A contract under which payment is received for performing a duty is considered paid; otherwise payment is not demanded, Civil Code 355. In a paid service, the performer carries out a service without a material form, and the customer pays, Civil Code 703.

t: Compensation for moral harm
n: Moral harm is physical and moral suffering resulting from an infringement of personal non-property rights or intangible benefits, Civil Code 1021. It is compensated in money. The court determines the amount reasonably and fairly, taking into account the nature of the suffering, the details of the circumstances, the characteristics of the victim and the degree of fault. Moral harm does not depend on property damage. Rudeness, disrespect and disclosure of medical confidentiality may also be grounds for it. If the will of an in-patient is certified by the chief physician, his deputy or the duty doctor, it is equated with a notarised one, Civil Code 1126.

t: The Law "On the Protection of Consumer Rights"
n: The law on the protection of consumer rights was adopted in 1996. In it, the medical worker or institution is considered the performer of a service and the patient the consumer. Article 4: the consumer receives full information about the service and the performer, freely chooses the service, and demands a quality and safe service and compensation for harm. Article 20: harm from a defect in a service, that is, harm to life, health or property, is compensated by the performer even if there was no contract. In case of force majeure or fault of the consumer, the performer is released. Article 22: if the performer is found at fault, he pays also for moral harm, irrespective of material damage. The court determines the amount of payment.

t: Case analysis: civil-law liability
n: A hypothetical situation: after a procedure the patient said his health had worsened and claimed treatment costs, lost wages and moral harm. The costs of medicines and treatment are actual damage, and lost wages are lost profit. In the dispute the court relies on a forensic medical examination. Fault is presumed: the burden of proving innocence falls on the clinic. This is why an original, complete medical record without corrections matters. Think about it: in which three cases will the clinic be found not guilty? Can rude treatment be grounds for moral harm even if there is no material damage?

t: Conclusion: distinguishing the three liabilities
n: To conclude: we distinguish three liabilities. In disciplinary liability, the penalty is a reprimand, a fine of up to 30% of the average monthly wage, or termination of the contract. The penalty is applied within one month of the offence being discovered. In administrative liability, medical workers most often receive a fine; an example is violation of sanitary and anti-epidemic rules, and liability begins at age 16. The aim of civil liability is to compensate for harm; fault is presumed, and the general limitation period is three years. Attention: being held to another type of liability does not release one from compensating for harm. In practice, informed consent and complete documentation are protective.
